I like your point and you're right. So taking it further, consider that these "mass sites" serve as safe walled-gardens for lazy people to find "content" and are of course naturally magnets for propaganda and censorship - in fact, defining the parameters of discussion (or say, restricting mass interaction to controlled sites) is the goal. Think of Reddit 2014 as a net designed to catch almost everybody and show only certain things. Facebook has of course admitted to researching mood manipulation and such via their news feed.

The solution then is to destroy those places any time they appear. By preventing the existence of large, sanctioned places where "everything" is posted people are forced to actually go in search of things on their own, inevitably leading to vastly greater information freedom. It's also how the web used to function for a long time. So instead of creating a better version of the mass-site we need to simply undermine mass sites in general.

I have not thought in that direction before. But I believe that an offensive strategy like an attack on sites like facebook and reddit would cause more disagreement and fuel stronger reactions than to draw users away by offering something more compelling.

Rather than destroying reddit and having to repeat that each time a new site comes up, it might be more sustainable to build something that is inherently safe from control through single organizations and that feels to the users of the currently dominating sites as a natural progression that they want to follow. Making the bad guys obsolete is imho a better aproach than making them martyrs.
The only decentralized alternative to reddit that I've heard of thus far is aether, and it's not really usable right now. We definitely need more competition in this space.
